series: HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK — PART 3

slides.page_title: Hostname Verification and What Clients Must Check

items: Match SAN dNSName against the URL hostname
Not the IP, not the redirect target
Wildcards cover the leftmost label only
`ap*.example.com` partial-label is not accepted
A wildcard never matches across a dot
IP literal connections need an iPAddress SAN
A dNSName entry does not cover an IP
Trailing dot `example.com.` trips naive matchers
IDN / punycode homographs are a bypass source
Each one disables authentication entirely
The connection is still encrypted
But encrypted to whoever answered
Which is exactly the attacker's position
Hard-code an expected leaf or intermediate key hash
Stops a rogue-CA attack cold
Rotate keys without a backup pin and you brick the app
HPKP was the web version and is dead
Mobile still pins, with backup pins and a kill switch
`Strict-Transport-Security` refuses plaintext for `max-age`
Closes the initial `http://` redirect hijack window
The preload list ships in the browser binary
It protects even the very first visit
Removal takes months — `preload` is near one-way

blocks.title: mTLS Flips It
items: Server sends a CertificateRequest
Client presents its own certificate
Standard for service-to-service and zero trust
The server must send a cert before it knows the site
The HTTP `Host:` header arrives after the handshake
SNI (RFC 6066) puts the hostname in ClientHello
So the server can pick the right certificate
Pre-SNI the workaround was one IP per HTTPS site
A real constraint that shaped early hosting prices
SNI is what enables shared hosting, CDNs, cloud LBs
Thousands of certs behind a single IP address
SNI is sent in the clear even in TLS 1.3
It rides in ClientHello, before any keys exist
Your ISP and your employer's proxy read it
So does any on-path observer, for free
Page content encrypted, destination name is not

blocks.title: Cheap To Censor
blocks.text: SNI-based blocking runs at national and corporate scale precisely because it is cheap: read one field, drop the packet.

items: Encrypted Client Hello encrypts the real ClientHello
Including SNI, under a key in the HTTPS DNS record
A decoy outer SNI goes in the clear
It only helps with a large anonymity set
A lone ECH-enabled origin is still identifiable

blocks.title: ECH Needs DNS Too
items: Without DoH or DoT the lookup leaks the hostname
That happens before TLS even starts
Encrypted DNS is a hard dependency, not a bonus
The old hack: benign SNI, real `Host:` inside
Major CDNs killed it by requiring the two to match
No SNI or wrong SNI gets the default cert
Symptom is a confusing hostname-mismatch error
nginx `server_name` selects the vhost by SNI
First `server` block on a listen address is fallback
A full handshake costs round trips plus asymmetric math
Resumption reuses an earlier session's secret
That skips both costs at once
One key encrypts every ticket you ever issue
Leak it and past sessions decrypt retroactively
That destroys forward secrecy after the fact
Rotate in hours, not months, and keep keys in memory
Many defaults never rotate — that is the trap

lines: # rotate keys; never back them to disk

items: Server sends `NewSessionTicket` after the handshake
The client uses it as a pre-shared key next time
Resumption is 1-RTT; `early_data` makes it 0-RTT
Pure PSK resumption has no forward secrecy
Add `psk_key_exchange_modes` with (EC)DHE to restore it

blocks.title: Early Data Replays
blocks.text: The server contributed no freshness, so an attacker can capture and re-send early data. Restrict it to idempotent requests or keep an anti-replay window.

caption.text: Part 3 of HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK. The padlock does not mean the site is safe — it means the bytes are encrypted to whoever answered the phone. This handbook walks the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes packet by packet, decodes certificate chains and SAN matching, explains why SNI still leaks every hostname you visit, and ends with the config checklist and error-triage table you actually reach for at 2am. 10 pages, no fluff: internals, trade-offs, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.
